questions.q: Name the three types of meristematic tissues classified on the basis of their location in the plant body.
questions.a: The three types are **apical meristem** (at root and shoot tips), **lateral meristem** (along the sides of stems and roots, e.g., vascular cambium and cork cambium), and **intercalary meristem** (at the base of nodes or internodes in grasses). A wrong answer that lists parenchyma, collenchyma, or sclerenchyma reveals confusion between meristematic and permanent tissue categories.

questions.q: Why do meristematic cells typically have dense cytoplasm, a prominent nucleus, thin cellulosic walls, and lack large vacuoles?
questions.a: These features support rapid cell division: dense cytoplasm and a large nucleus provide the metabolic machinery and genetic material for mitosis; thin walls allow easy expansion after division; absence of large vacuoles prevents mechanical hindrance to chromosome segregation. A wrong answer citing "storage of food" or "mechanical support" indicates the student is attributing permanent tissue functions to meristematic cells.

questions.q: A student examines a transverse section of a young stem under a microscope and observes vascular bundles arranged in a distinct ring. The bundles are conjoint, open, and show endarch protoxylem. Identify the plant group (monocot/dicot) and justify your answer using tissue organization.
questions.a: The stem is **dicotyledonous**. Reasoning: (1) Ring arrangement of vascular bundles is a hallmark of dicot stems. (2) Conjoint, open bundles with cambium allow secondary growth, typical of dicots. (3) Endarch protoxylem (maturing from centre to periphery) is characteristic of dicot stems. A wrong answer of "monocot" shows inability to link bundle arrangement and cambium presence to the correct plant group.

questions.q: Compare the functional roles of intercalary meristem in grasses with apical meristem in a dicot herb. How does their location relate to the plant's response to grazing or pruning?
questions.a: Apical meristem at the shoot tip drives primary elongation; if removed (pruning), the main stem stops lengthening but axillary buds may grow. Intercalary meristem at the base of nodes/internodes in grasses allows rapid regrowth of cut leaves and stems because the meristem remains below the grazing height. A wrong answer that states both are at the tips fails to recognize the adaptive significance of intercalary meristem location in monocots.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "All permanent tissues in plants are dead at maturity and provide only mechanical support."
questions.a: **False.** While sclerenchyma (fibres and sclereids) are dead at maturity and provide mechanical support, **parenchyma** remains living, thin-walled, and performs photosynthesis, storage, secretion, and wound healing. Collenchyma is also living and provides flexible support. A student who agrees with the statement has overgeneralized from sclerenchyma to all permanent tissues.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a germinating bean seed to demonstrate that root elongation occurs only in the region just behind the root tip (zone of elongation) and not uniformly along the root.
questions.a: Mark the radicle of a germinating bean seed with waterproof ink at 1 mm intervals. Allow it to grow for 24 hours. Measure the distance between marks: marks near the tip will have moved apart (elongation zone), while marks higher up remain unchanged. A good answer includes a control (unmarked seed) and notes that the meristematic zone itself (first 0.5–1 mm) shows little elongation. A poor answer merely states "measure root length daily" without spatial resolution.
